drapeaux.note: Hall's sentence is already in English in the French entry (The Friends of Voltaire, 1906, Project Gutenberg 56618); copied unchanged. The same English wording is used for the sentence quoted in the body.

Voltaire's exclamation reported by Hall is given in Hall's own English wording (“What a fuss about an omelette!” he had exclaimed when he heard of the burning), as reproduced in Quote Investigator (quoteinvestigator.com/2015/06/01/defend-say/); the Project Gutenberg text (ebook 56618) itself was not reachable during this repair.

titre: “I Will Defend to the Death Your Right to Say It”: It Is Not Voltaire
accroche: The motto of free speech dates from 1906: an English biographer was summing up Voltaire's attitude, without claiming to quote him.
contenu_vulgarise:
“I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.” The sentence is spread across posters, speeches, and textbooks, always signed Voltaire. It is not his.

## A Book of 1906

The sentence appears in *The Friends of Voltaire*, published in London in 1906 by Evelyn Beatrice Hall under the pseudonym S. G. Tallentyre. It is found in the chapter devoted to Helvétius. Helvétius's book, *De l'esprit* (*On the Mind*), has just been condemned and burned; Hall tells how Helvétius, pressed by his friends and by his mother to retract, publishes a letter of apology; the Parlement (a royal high court) condemns him to give up his office and exiles him for two years. Voltaire, for his part, comes to his defense. Hall writes that he exclaimed “What a fuss about an omelette!”, then adds: “‘I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it,’ was his attitude now.”

The key word is “attitude.” Hall does not claim to report a line of dialogue: she sums up, in quotation marks, a position that she attributes to Voltaire.

## How a Paraphrase Becomes a Quotation

The quotation marks did the rest. Detached from its chapter, the sentence circulated as a saying of Voltaire's. In 1943, the scholar Burdette Kinne devoted a short note to it, titled “Voltaire Never Said it!”, in *Modern Language Notes*. The study finds that the sentence is not his; reference works on false quotations, such as *They Never Said It* (Boller and George, Oxford University Press, 1989), place it among the erroneous attributions.

## What It Shifts

Saying that the sentence is not Voltaire's tells us nothing about his tolerance: only that the formula is that of a biographer of 1906. Hall herself reports, in the same passage, that persecution made *De l'esprit* one of the most famous books of the century, where it would otherwise have been only a success of the season. The apocryphal quotation follows the same path: by dint of being repeated, an idea changes author. The process is common: a quotation mark is enough to turn a summary into reported speech, and a flattering summary into a trophy. What we take for a cry from the 18th century is a summary written nearly a century and a half later.

quiz.question: Where does the sentence “I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it” come from?
choix: From a letter from Voltaire to Helvétius, written in 1759
From the Treatise on Tolerance, published by Voltaire in 1763
From the Philosophical Dictionary, article “Tolerance,” of 1764
From a biography of Voltaire published in London in 1906
quiz.explication: Evelyn Beatrice Hall wrote it in 1906 to sum up Voltaire's attitude toward the condemnation of Helvétius's book. No attestation of it is known in Voltaire himself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which word in Hall's text shows that she is not reporting an exact line of dialogue?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Hall writes that such was his “attitude”: she sums up a position, she does not quote words that were spoken.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Helvétius face after the condemnation of his book De l'esprit?
choix: He is imprisoned in the Bastille for six months
He has to leave France permanently for England
He publishes a letter of apology and the Parlement exiles him for two years
He is forced to burn his remaining copies himself
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Pressed by his friends and his mother, Helvétius publishes a letter of apology; the Parlement takes away his office and exiles him for two years, the entry says.
